query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In highly aggressive chemical and nuclear service environments, increasing the chromium content in steel promotes the rapid formation of a thin, uniform, and stable Cr2O3 passivation layer that significantly enhances corrosion resistance relative to steels with standard chromium levels.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional corrosion‐resistant steels with industry typical chromium content and microstructure.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the chromium content in the steel samples.
generation.conditions: Exposure to controlled high-temperature and aggressive chemical environments (e.g., molten salts or chloride‐rich aqueous media) that simulate chemical-processing and nuclear-power operational conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 passive film on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: A higher chromium content increases the availability of Cr atoms at the steel surface, which oxidize preferentially to form a stable Cr2O3 film. This film acts as a barrier to corrosive species, reducing localized dissolution and overall corrosion rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels with elevated chromium levels will develop a more uniform and thicker Cr2O3 film, resulting in reduced corrosion rates (evidenced by lower weight loss and fewer pits) relative to baseline steels with standard chromium content.
generation.baseline: Steels with standard, industry typical chromium content that form thinner or less uniform passive films.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid under aggressive, high-temperature environments typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications; performance may vary under ambient or less aggressive conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the enhanced performance is predicted, the magnitude of the corrosion resistance improvement may be influenced by other factors such as microstructural variations and the presence of minor alloying elements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of steel samples with systematically increased chromium content. Expose all samples, along with a baseline standard steel, to a corrosive environment (either a molten salt bath or a chloride-rich aqueous solution) under controlled temperature and time. Ensure uniform sample geometry and surface preparation.
measurements: Weight loss tests to quantify overall corrosion rate.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements to assess corrosion kinetics.
Surface analysis via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) or scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to characterize the thickness, uniformity, and chemical composition of the passive Cr2O3 layer.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If steels with higher chromium content do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the formation of a uniform and thick Cr2O3 passivation layer, nor a measurable reduction in corrosion rate compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis that elevated chromium enhances corrosion resistance by forming a protective Cr2O3 film is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].

drafts.hypothesis: Increasing the chromium content in steel promotes the formation of a thin, stable chromium oxide passivation layer that is responsible for enhancing corrosion resistance in chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
drafts.material_initial_state: Steel alloys with a range of chromium concentrations (including a standard composition sample) in a typical microstructure.
drafts.intervention: Systematically vary the chromium content in the steel samples.
drafts.conditions: Expose the samples to controlled environments that replicate the aggressive chemical and thermal conditions typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications (e.g., elevated temperature, high humidity, and chemical oxidants).
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation and stability of a thin, adherent chromium oxide layer on the steel surface.
drafts.mechanism: Higher chromium levels enable chromium atoms to segregate to the steel surface during exposure, forming a uniform and chemically stable oxide film that passivates the metal and effectively reduces active corrosion sites.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Steel samples with higher chromium content will develop more uniform and thicker protective chromium oxide layers, leading to significantly lower corrosion rates compared to the baseline standard composition sample under the same test conditions.
drafts.baseline: Steel samples with a standard (industry typical) chromium concentration exposed to the same aggressive conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under moderate to high temperature, high humidity, and oxidizing conditions that mimic those in chemical-processing and nuclear-power plant environments; extreme conditions outside these ranges may introduce additional corrosion mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple steel samples with systematically varied chromium concentrations. Subject all samples to simulated aggressive environments replicating chemical-processing and nuclear conditions. Use standardized procedures to measure the formation, thickness, and uniformity of the oxide layer, as well as the corresponding corrosion rates.
measurements: Oxide film characterization via electron microscopy and surface analysis techniques
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to determine corrosion rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no systematic trend is observed where increased chromium content results in more stable or thicker chromium oxide layers accompanied by reduced corrosion rates compared to the baseline sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily due to the formation of a thin, adherent chromium oxide (Cr2O3) passivation film that develops on the steel surface when a sufficient amount of chromium is alloyed into the steel.
drafts.material_initial_state: Steels with varying concentrations of chromium alloying elements (including standard low-chromium and high-chromium formulations) in as-fabricated condition.
drafts.intervention: Expose the different steel samples to a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., high humidity, aggressive chemicals, and elevated temperatures representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions) designed to mimic operational stress.
drafts.conditions: Controlled laboratory conditions with identical temperature, humidity, chemical exposure, and time for each sample; tests should focus on environments relevant to both chemical processing and nuclear power applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 layer on the steel surface acting as a physical barrier to oxidation and corrosive species.
drafts.mechanism: Chromium in the alloy oxidizes preferentially under corrosive conditions to form a protective Cr2O3 film, which inhibits further penetration of corrosive agents into the underlying steel structure, thereby reducing corrosion rates.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Steels with higher chromium content will develop a more continuous and thicker Cr2O3 passivation film, leading to significantly lower corrosion rates compared to steels with lower chromium content. Relative to the baseline (low-chromium steel), high-chromium steels should show measurable improvements in corrosion resistance as evidenced by lower weight loss, less pitting, and reduced chemical degradation.
drafts.baseline: The corrosion performance and surface characteristics of low-chromium steels under identical corrosive conditions, where minimal or discontinuous passive layer formation is expected.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for steels manufactured with chromium levels within the typical ranges used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power installations; results might differ if non-standard alloying elements or extreme operating conditions are applied.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of steel samples with varying chromium contents (including low- and high-chromium formulations). Expose all samples to a standardized corrosive test environment representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions over an extended period. Periodically measure corrosion rates through weight loss, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and surface analyses (e.g., X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for film characterization).
measurements: Quantitative weight loss per unit area over time
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy readings to infer corrosion rate differences
Surface characterization data (XPS, SEM) indicating the presence, continuity, and composition of the oxide films
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-chromium steel samples do not show a significantly lower corrosion rate than low-chromium samples, or if surface analysis fails to reveal a continuous and compositionally consistent Cr2O3 passivation layer despite identical exposure conditions, the hypothesis that the Cr2O3 film confers the observed corrosion resistance will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In corrosive environments typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, steels gain enhanced corrosion resistance through minor additions of sacrificial elements (such as Al or Mn) that promote the formation of a stable, Cr‐enriched passive film. These sacrificial elements react preferentially with corrosive species to form compounds (e.g., AlCl3 or Mn oxides) at the alloy surface, creating a redox buffer that limits the dissolution of the key protective element (Cr) from the substrate.
drafts.material_initial_state: Conventional corrosion‐resistant steel with a baseline Cr content, produced with and without small additions of a sacrificial element (e.g., low-level Al or Mn).
drafts.intervention: Modify the steel composition by incorporating a controlled, minor amount of a sacrificial element and compare its behavior to an otherwise identical steel without the additive.
drafts.conditions: Exposure in controlled high-temperature corrosive environments representative of chemical processing or nuclear-power applications (for example, molten salt environments at 450–650 °C or aggressive chloride-containing aqueous media).
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of a self-healing, protective passivation film that is enriched in Cr and contains compounds of the sacrificial element, which together stabilize the film and slow further corrosion.
drafts.mechanism: The sacrificial element preferentially reacts with the aggressive media to form stable compounds at the interface; these compounds act as a redox buffer that preserves the integrity of the Cr2O3 passive layer, reducing further dissolution of Cr and maintaining the overall corrosion resistance of the steel.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline steel, the modified steel with sacrificial element additions will display a more uniform and stable passivation film, lower corrosion rates (evidenced by reduced weight loss and shallower corrosion penetration), and less Cr depletion from the surface layers after exposure.
drafts.baseline: Steel with conventional composition (i.e., without the sacrificial element addition), which forms a passive film primarily based on Cr without the added redox buffering effects.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under high-temperature, highly aggressive chemical environments (molten salts or high chlorides) typical of chemical processing and nuclear power; its benefit may be less noticeable under ambient or less aggressive conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples—one with a controlled low addition of a sacrificial element (e.g., Al or Mn) and one without. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature aggressive environments (such as a molten salt bath at 450–650 °C or a chloride-rich solution) for a fixed duration. Use consistent sample geometry and pre-treatment to control for extraneous variables.
measurements: Corrosion rate measurement via weight loss tests and/or electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS).
Surface analysis by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) to assess the composition and thickness of the passive film and quantify Cr depletion.
Microscopic imaging (SEM/TEM) to observe the uniformity and integrity of the passive layer.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the steel with sacrificial element addition does not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate, Cr depletion, and degradation of the passive film (compared to the baseline steel) or if no evidence of the expected redox buffering compounds is detected in the passive film, then the hypothesis that sacrificial element-induced redox buffering governs the enhanced corrosion resistance is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, the primary mechanism for corrosion resistance is the rapid formation and continuous repair of a protective chromium oxide (Cr2O3) passivation film. This film is enhanced by microstructural features—such as refined (fine-grained) structures—that promote faster Cr diffusion to the surface, thereby limiting localized dissolution and pitting.
drafts.material_initial_state: Conventional high-Cr stainless steels or duplex steels with a standard coarse-grained microstructure and nominal Cr content typical for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
drafts.intervention: Thermomechanical processing to produce steels with refined (ultrafine or nanocrystalline) grain structures and/or controlled variations in Cr content, followed by exposure to corrosive environments representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power service conditions.
drafts.conditions: Controlled laboratory corrosion tests using simulated environments (e.g., chloride-containing aqueous solutions or molten salt baths) at service-relevant temperatures (up to about 700 °C) and pressures.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation and stability of a contiguous and enriched Cr2O3 passivation layer, which is facilitated by high-density grain boundaries that act as fast diffusion pathways for Cr atoms.
drafts.mechanism: The refined grain structure increases the rate at which Cr atoms diffuse to the surface, enabling the rapid formation of a stable, self-healing Cr2O3 film that prevents further oxidation and the dissolution of less noble elements. This dynamic repair mechanism limits pit initiation and overall corrosion progress under aggressive conditions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Steels processed to have a finer grain structure and optimized Cr content will exhibit a thicker, more uniform, and more stable Cr2O3 film. This will result in lower corrosion current densities, reduced pit density, and slower overall mass loss compared to baseline coarse-grained steels under identical corrosive conditions.
drafts.baseline: Standard, coarse-grained high-Cr steels used in these applications without additional microstructure refinement or Cr diffusion enhancement.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in environments typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power systems (such as chloride-rich aqueous solutions and molten salt environments) and within a moderate temperature range (up to approximately 700 °C). The contribution of other alloying elements (e.g., Ni or Mo) is acknowledged but is assumed to play a secondary role in this specific passivation mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of steel samples with varying grain sizes (via controlled thermomechanical processing) and with different Cr contents. Expose these samples to a corrosive environment (e.g., a 0.6 M NaCl solution or a molten salt bath) under controlled temperature and pressure conditions that mimic service environments. Use surface analysis techniques (such as XPS and SEM) to measure the thickness, uniformity, and composition of the passivation layer and electrochemical methods (such as EIS) to assess corrosion rates.
measurements: Grain size and microstructure via metallography or electron microscopy
Cr2O3 layer thickness and composition via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
Corrosion current density and impedance via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)
Pit density and morphology via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with refined grain structure and higher Cr content do not exhibit a significantly thicker, more uniform, and more stable Cr2O3 passivation film, or if their corrosion rates (as measured by lower corrosion current density, fewer pits, or reduced mass loss) are not notably improved relative to baseline samples, the proposed mechanism that enhanced Cr diffusion leading to superior passivation is falsified.
